say.text: Your classmate Ravi is revising burn fluids. His note says: “Burns need 4 mL × kg × %TBSA, every time. The formula is the answer.”
The stem you are revising says “as per current practice”. What do you tell Ravi?

choices.label: Keep 4 mL: it is the rule for every burn fluid question
4 mL is the exam key; current practice starts lower, then titrates
Keep 4 mL, then hold the same rate after 8 hours
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at one word in the stem: “current”. Ask what that word changes about the starting figure, then what the rate depends on after that.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because 4 mL is the figure PYQs have printed, so it feels like the only formula you need.
The stem’s qualifier decides which practice the question means, and a formula is only a starting point. Try again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one matters: a memorised formula is the belief most likely to stick. Read the qualifier before you trust the number.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because a fixed start looks like a complete order, and the formula does give you a start.
But the rate is changed hour by hour to urine output, not held after the first 8 hours. Try again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the rate itself: a fixed rate is the habit to unlearn.

say.text: Here is the reason, with the claims behind it.
PYQs have expected 4 mL per kg per %TBSA. The word “current” asks for the practice that starts lower, about 2 mL in adults, and then titrates to urine output.
So the formula is a start, and the qualifier tells you which start to use.
Ravi again: “Burns leak protein, so give albumin from the first hour, whichever formula you use.”
Which line do you give him for classic Parkland in the first 24 hours?

choices.label: Parkland and Evans differ only in how much albumin they add
Albumin from the first hour, because burns leak protein out
Parkland uses Ringer lactate alone for the first 24 hours
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Name the formula first. Ask which of the named formulae adds colloid, and whether classic Parkland is one of them.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because Evans and Brooke look like Parkland with albumin added, so the names blur together.
Each formula has its own fluid mix, and Evans is not a version of Parkland. Try again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this blur is the one to fix: the formulae are separate recipes, not variants of one.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because burns do leak protein, so albumin feels like the right fluid from hour one.
Albumin is not part of classic Parkland’s first 24 hours; colloid is considered later, if at all. Try again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the timing: colloid is not part of classic Parkland’s first day.

say.text: Here is the reason, with the claims behind it.
Classic Parkland gives crystalloid alone in the first 24 hours, Ringer lactate. Colloid is considered later, if the capillary leak persists or needs are very high.
Evans and Brooke are the formulae that add colloid, so keep them apart from Parkland.
Ravi’s rule for every smoke victim: “Give 100% oxygen and the smoke poisons are covered.”
What is the correct pairing you give him instead?

choices.label: Cyanide needs 100% oxygen, and CO needs hydroxocobalamin
Calcium gluconate for cyanide, as for other chemical burns
CO needs 100% oxygen, and cyanide needs hydroxocobalamin
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what each poison does in the body, then match its own antidote. A shared word like “smoke” should not decide the pairing.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because both poisons come from the same fire, so one gas feels as if it needs one treatment.
Each poison has its own antidote, and swapping the two is the usual slip. Try again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is the swap to watch: the two poisons are the ones people pair the wrong way round.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because both are poisonings or chemical injuries, so calcium feels like a general antidote.
Calcium gluconate belongs to a different poison, the hydrofluoric acid burn. Try again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pin each antidote to its own poison: calcium gluconate is not a smoke antidote.

say.text: Here is the reason, with the claims behind it.
Carbon monoxide is treated with 100% oxygen, and hyperbaric oxygen is kept for selected cases. Cyanide from smoke is treated with hydroxocobalamin.
One shared fire does not mean one antidote. Pair each poison with its own.
Ravi: “For an ear burn, use silver sulfadiazine, since it goes deepest into the eschar.”
What do you correct, and which agent goes with the ear?

choices.label: Mafenide penetrates eschar best, so it suits ear cartilage
Silver sulfadiazine penetrates eschar best, so it suits ears
Silver nitrate penetrates eschar, and it suits the ear
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which agent is known for going through eschar, and which one is the painless broad cover. Then match each to its property.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because silver sulfadiazine is the agent most often used, so it feels like the default for everything.
Its strengths are broad cover and little pain, with leucopenia as its side effect; deep penetration belongs to another agent. Try again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is a pairing slip: the default agent is not the eschar-penetrating one.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because silver nitrate is a familiar silver agent, and students blur the silver names together.
Silver nitrate is known for the black stain and for hyponatraemia, not for going through eschar. Try again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-pair each agent with its own side effect; the eschar property belongs to one agent.

say.text: Here is the reason, with the claims behind it.
Mafenide penetrates eschar, which is why it suits ear cartilage. Its side effect is metabolic acidosis.
Silver sulfadiazine is the broad, painless default, and its side effect is leucopenia.
Ravi’s note: “Curling’s ulcer is the cancer that grows in an old scar, and Marjolin’s is the stress ulcer in the stomach.”
What do you tell him about the two ulcers?

choices.label: They are one ulcer seen at two times, so the names overlap
Curling’s is the early gut ulcer; Marjolin’s is the late scar cancer
Curling’s is the late scar cancer; Marjolin’s the early gut ulcer
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Sort each name by two things: the organ it sits in, and how long after the burn it appears.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because both names mention a burn, so the early and late labels feel swappable.
Marjolin’s is not the stress ulcer: it is a cancer that arises late in a chronic scar. Try again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the swap is the risk: sort the names by site and timing, not by the shared word burn.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because both ulcers follow burns, so people link them as one complication.
They are separate entities: one is an acute gut ulcer, and the other is a late cancer in a scar. Try again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep them apart: one belongs to the gut and the early weeks, the other to a scar and the late course.

say.text: Here is the reason, with the claims behind it.
Curling’s ulcer is an acute stress ulcer of the stomach or duodenum after major burns, so it is an early complication.
Marjolin’s ulcer is squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic burn scar, so it belongs to the late course.
Ravi: “Any deep burn wrapped around a limb needs an escharotomy at once.”
What is your correction?

choices.label: Any deep partial-thickness burn, since eschar forms in every deep burn
Only full-thickness circumferential burns that compromise limb or chest
Any circumferential burn, since the ring itself is the problem
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Two things decide it: how deep the burn is, and whether the ring of eschar is actually cutting off circulation or ventilation.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because eschar does form in deep burns, so depth feels like the whole reason.
Escharotomy is aimed at full-thickness burns, where the eschar cannot stretch; partial thickness is not the target. Try again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pin the depth qualifier: deep alone is not enough.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because a ring of burn looks dangerous whatever its depth.
A ring alone is not enough: release is needed when it is full thickness and the eschar constricts. Try again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check both qualifiers together: depth, and whether the eschar is constricting.

say.text: Here is the reason, with the claims behind it.
Full-thickness skin does not stretch. As oedema builds, a circumferential eschar on a limb or chest constricts and cuts off circulation or ventilation.
Release is made through the eschar only, along the midlateral and midaxial lines, and it can often be done at the bedside.
